tomato_early_blight.description: A common fungal disease affecting tomato foliage, stems, and fruit, typically appearing on older, lower leaves first and progressing upward.
symptoms: Small, dark brown to black spots on lower/older leaves
Spots develop concentric rings, giving a 'target board' appearance
Yellowing (chlorosis) of leaf tissue surrounding spots
Premature leaf drop, starting from the bottom of the plant
Dark, sunken lesions may appear on stems and fruit
prevention: Rotate crops — avoid planting tomatoes/potatoes in the same soil for 2-3 years
Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Space plants adequately to improve air circulation
Avoid overhead irrigation; water at the base of the plant
Remove and destroy infected plant debris after harvest
Mulch around the base of plants to reduce soil splash onto leaves

organic: Copper-based fungicides, applied per product label

safety_notes: Always follow the product label for dosage and pre-harvest intervals — this system does not provide dosages
Wear appropriate protective equipment when applying any fungicide
Consult your local agricultural extension office before applying chemical treatments
Rotate fungicide classes to avoid resistance buildup

tomato_late_blight.description: An aggressive water-mold disease capable of destroying entire tomato and potato crops within days under cool, wet conditions.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked greenish-black lesions on leaves
White, fuzzy fungal growth on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Rapid browning and collapse of foliage
Dark, firm, greasy-looking lesions on fruit
Distinct musty odor from severely infected plants
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation and excess humidity around plants
Ensure good airflow through proper spacing and pruning
Monitor weather — risk increases sharply in cool, wet, humid conditions
Destroy volunteer potato/tomato plants which can harbor the pathogen

organic: Copper-based fungicides applied preventively before disease onset
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to slow spread

safety_notes: Late blight spreads extremely fast — isolate/remove infected plants immediately
This system does not provide dosages; follow local agricultural guidance
Consult a plant pathologist or extension officer for confirmation, as late blight can be confused with other blights

potato_early_blight.description: A fungal disease of potato foliage and tubers, closely related to tomato early blight, most damaging to stressed or nutrient-deficient plants.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric ring patterns on lower leaves
Yellow halo surrounding lesions
Leaves become brittle and drop prematurely
Dark, sunken, dry lesions on tubers with slightly raised borders
prevention: Rotate crops with non-solanaceous plants for at least 2 years
Maintain balanced soil fertility — nitrogen-stressed plants are more susceptible
Avoid overhead watering; irrigate early in the day if unavoidable
Hill soil properly to reduce tuber exposure to spores

organic: Compost tea foliar applications to support plant immune response

safety_notes: Follow product label instructions strictly — no dosage recommendations are given here
Observe pre-harvest intervals before consuming treated tubers
Consult your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra or agricultural extension office

potato_late_blight.description: The same pathogen responsible for the historic Irish potato famine; remains one of the most economically damaging potato diseases worldwide.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale to dark green lesions on leaf tips and edges
Lesions quickly turn brown to black and expand rapidly
White fungal growth visible on leaf undersides in humid weather
Reddish-brown dry rot inside infected tubers
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes
Plant resistant varieties where available
Improve field drainage and avoid excess irrigation
Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants that can harbor spores over winter

organic: Preventive copper-based fungicide applications before wet weather periods
chemical: Fungicides containing mandipropamid, chlorothalonil, or cymoxanil, applied preventively

safety_notes: This disease can devastate a field within days — early reporting to an extension officer is critical
This system does not provide dosages; follow local agricultural authority guidance
Destroy severely infected plants to prevent spread to healthy fields

rice_leaf_blast.description: One of the most destructive fungal diseases of rice worldwide, capable of affecting leaves, nodes, necks, and panicles.
symptoms: Small, diamond/spindle-shaped lesions with gray-white centers and brown margins
Lesions may merge, causing entire leaves to wither
Grayish lesions at nodes, causing stems to break easily
Neck rot at panicle base, leading to empty or partially filled grains
prevention: Use resistant rice varieties suited to your region
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which increases susceptibility
Maintain proper field water management — avoid drought stress
Ensure balanced spacing to reduce humidity buildup in the canopy
Remove and destroy infected crop residue after harvest

organic: Silicon-based soil amendments to strengthen cell walls (supportive, not curative)

safety_notes: This system does not provide dosages — always follow local agricultural extension recommendations
Confirm diagnosis with a local expert where possible, as blast can resemble brown spot disease
Avoid fungicide overuse; rotate active ingredients to prevent resistance

Practice crop rotation as a preventive measure even when no disease is present
